title: Personalised diagnosis and treatment for refractory focal epilepsy
summary:
Motivation

Epilepsy is one of the most common neurological diseases. There are forms of epilepsy,
in which the seizures originate in only a small part of the brain (so-called "focal epilepsies").
They account for about two-thirds of all epilepsies.  Epilepsies can often be treated well with medication but in about one-third of all patients with epilepsy, seizure freedom is not achieved with medication. Also, and especially in the case of focal epilepsies, medications often do not work
as desired, so that alternative treatments are needed. One possible approach is to use brain activity measurements (electroencephalogram, EEG) to find the so-called epileptogenic zone, i.e., the origin of the seizures. If it can be identified, it can be surgically removed or destroyed. However, often the epileptogenic zone cannot be localized precisely enough or it overlaps with brain areas that control elementary functions such as the ability to speak and therefore surgery is not possible. Epilepsy surgery is currently only an option for 15 to 20 percent of those affected - the rest are dependent on medication that might have only limited effect.

Goals and procedure

Four universities from three European countries (Germany, Finnland and France) have joined forces in the PerEpi project to develop improved methods for the diagnosis and treatment of focal epilepsy.

Instead of the previously used EEG, a combination of a high-resolution EEG and two other imaging methods will now provide more accurate results. By combining data that depict not only electrical activity but also the magnetic fields that occur (magnetoencephalogram, MEG), complex mathematical-physical calculations can be used to optimize the localization of the epileptogenic zone in the brain. This method offers several advantages: Thanks to this method, not only can the chance of success of an operation be increased, but also the number of patients for whom a surgical intervention is possible at all - because the epileptogenic zone must be known for this.

What is special about the PerEpi project is that it only deals with procedures that do not involve physical penetration of the patient's body (so-called non-invasive procedures). In addition to the method for determining the epileptogenic zone, the research group is also working on an innovative and practically non-invasive brain stimulation therapy: the method is intended to reduce the number and severity of seizures by using electrodes attached to the scalp to administer individually adapted currents to the patient.

Perspectives for practice

The methods explored in this project are expected to form the basis for further development work that, in the long term, will help to better determine the epileptogenic zone in the brain of individual patients. In addition, the electric stimulation investigated here could help patients whose epilepsy disease cannot be treated either by medication or surgery. If these two steps succeed, more patients may be treated by epilepsy surgery or brain stimulation in the future, in addition to medication.

interventions.name:
Experimental: 
Individually optimized multi-channel transcranial direct current stimulation (mc-tDCS):
2 x 20 min of mc-tDCS with 20 min pause inbetween at 4 mA distributed over multiple electrodes and individually targeted to the epileptogenic zone once daily over 5 consecutive days.

Sham Comparator: 
Active sham stimulation 
2 x 20 min of active sham mc-tDCS with 20 min pause inbetween at 4 mA (feeling at skin level is similar to real stimulation, but nearly no current reaches the epileptogenic zone) distributed and administered over multiple electrodes once daily over 5 cons

criteria:
Inclusion criteria:
- Adult male and female subjects between 18 and 70 years of age
- New patients, but also previously studied patients  who are not yet seizure-free
- Classification of the epileptogenic foci and possibility of a high quality reconstruction of the epileptogenic zone, i.e. sufficient ictal and interictal measured and reconstructable activity of sufficient signal-to-noise ratio, sufficient overlap of the irritative zone with the epileptogenic zone and with possible lesions in the MRI
- Number and severity of seizures occurring and how they might be affected by stimulation and/or surgery.
- Sufficiently high average weekly seizure frequencies.
- Usually there is enough time between diagnosis and surgery that mc-tDCS can be interposed. However, if there is not enough time, surgery should not normally be postponed. For the tDCS this would mean a drop out, but the diagnostic part of PerEpi could be successfully validated. However, if the treating physicians decide that the surgery will be delayed in order to enable mc-tDCS first, then this would be discussed and considered with the patient)

Additional inclusion criteria include:
- countable seizures
- Pat. or relatives notice the seizures
- Patients or relatives are able to keep a seizure diary.
- Patients are particularly eligible if either no surgery / resection can be offered after pre-surgical diagnosis or if the patient does not (yet) want surgery.
- Severity of seizures: motor or non-motor; conscious seizures or not (following the terminology in the current seizure classification of the ILAE); seizures with or without loss of body postural control.
Exclusion criteria:
- Seizures that cannot be counted
- Seizures that are not noticed by the patient or relatives to a relevant extent.
- Metal in or on the body
- Head too large for combined EEG/MEG measurement

Drop-outs could be caused by too much movement in EEG/MEG/MRI, so that data quality is too poor or that targeting is not possible (e.g. because not enough ictal and interictal activity could be measured or because the reconstructions cannot be trusted due to poor signal-to-noise ratio). We will try to replace the drop outs with more incoming patients.
